chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: Minton's Playhouse: Teddy Hill makes him bandleader
summary: Hill, managing Minton's, made Clarke bandleader with Monk, Joe Guy and Nick Fenton; Monday hash dinners drew Apollo performers and Big Sid Catlett called his drumming modern.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Well, what happened? Where did you go?
Well, immediately after that happened, Teddy took over Minton's Playhouse.
Oh, yeah. That's right.
And to make it up to me, which he thought
he had done, he had done wrong, he didn't think that I deserved to be fired.
Yeah. Teddy was -- Teddy had a progressive mind, didn't he?
Oh, he was so far ahead. So he said -- well, he was listening to these old guys, like Henry Wood and those guys.
Yeah.

You know. But after he became manager of this club, he came and got me. He said, 'Now, Kenny, I'm managing this place. I want you to be the band leader. You play all the re-bop and the boom-bams you want to play.' So I said, oh, this is wonderful, you know.
(Laughter)
He said, 'You can drop all the bombs, all this re-bop, or whatever you all are playing,' you know. He said, 'You can do it here.' So, okay, we took Joe Guy, Monk, Nick Fenton.
Oh, Nick Fenton.
The bass player. And he played wonderful violin, too.
Oh?
And we started this group at Teddy's. So then we began to play all the things that we had always wanted to play for so long, and now we had a chance.
So Monk -- because Monk was kind of good (unintelligible).

Yeah, Monk was great. And we started with this rhythm section, with Joe Guy. Every Monday Teddy would have a hash dinner, you know, for the people appearing at the Apollo Theater. So then every Monday, everybody would, after the show, everyone was hungry, so they would come to Teddy's to have hash and biscuits and all that.
Yeah.
So we began to play our things. So everybody began to listen.
Yeah.
Said, "What is that little drummer up there doing?" So Big Sid said, "Man, that little cat is modern, if you listen to him." So that was the biggest sendoff. That was the stamp I needed.
Yeah. Isn't that beautiful.
So ever since then the more the drummers became interested the more I tried to develop it, you know. Not to the point where they couldn't understand it.
No.
But bring it to a point where --
Where it might catch.
Catch, and make it interesting.
